passage: At the badminton club's front desk, Arnab slid a laminated card across to Gopika. Weekday mornings: ₹1,500 a month. All-day access: ₹2,800. All-day with a locker: ₹2,850. "Most people take the last one," he said. Gopika smiled, laid her palm flat over the middle line and looked only at the other two. Then she took out the notebook she had brought and read her own list aloud: "Budget, two thousand. Play before work, three days a week. No locker needed, I live five minutes away." She looked up. "Weekday mornings, please." Arnab raised his eyebrows. "Most people don't say no to the locker." "Most people didn't write a list first," she said, and signed.

qa.q: What did Gopika lay her palm over?
qa.a: The middle line on the card, the all-day access plan.

qa.q: Why do you think Gopika brought a written list to the club?
qa.a: She seemed to expect the offer's layout might push her, so she wanted her own budget and needs written down beforehand to decide by them.

qa.q: Which steps made Gopika's choice sound?
qa.a: Covering the option nobody would pick, then reading her own list, a budget, morning play and no need for a locker, and choosing the plan that matched it.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel when Gopika picks the cheapest plan?
qa.a: Arnab seems surprised, since most people take the locker plan, and may notice for the first time how much the card's layout usually does the choosing.

grounding: A young woman covers the option nobody would pick and chooses a club plan by her own written budget and needs, not the layout of the offer.

passage:
Hi Mahima,
You asked how I finally chose a laptop. The secret is a pencil. The website showed three: one with 8 GB memory for ₹42,000, one with 16 GB for ₹61,000, and one with 16 GB plus a bigger screen for ₹62,000. Everything on the page was designed to make me want the last one. So I printed the page and struck through the ₹61,000 one, because nobody would ever choose it. Then I wrote my own list: budget ₹50,000, spreadsheets and video calls, light enough for the train. Against that list, the ₹42,000 one wins easily. The big-screen one would have been lovely and wrong. Try the pencil when you pick your phone.
Deepak

qa.q: What was Deepak's budget?
What did Deepak think the website was trying to do?
qa.a: Deepak felt wary, sensing the page was built to push the ₹62,000 laptop by using the ₹61,000 one to make it look like a bargain.

qa.q: Why was striking through the middle option useful before writing the list?
qa.a: Once the option nobody would choose was gone, the bigger laptop stopped looking like a deal, so Deepak could compare the rest against Deepak's own budget and needs.

qa.q: How might Mahima use this email when choosing a phone?
qa.a: Mahima could list the options, cross out any that seem to be there only to push another, and write down Mahima's own needs first.

grounding: A young adult strikes out the decoy option and chooses a laptop by a written list of their own budget and needs.

passage: Wasim, the caterer tried the oldest trick on me. I'm Suraj, the brother in charge of food for my sister's engagement, and I had three packages: Simple at ₹350 a plate, Deluxe at ₹620, and Royal at ₹640 with two extra sweets and a live counter. The owner kept tapping Royal. "Twenty rupees more, sir, and so much more!" I asked for a minute, took a photo of the menu card, went out to the car and covered Deluxe with my thumb on the screen. Then I opened the note I'd made with Amma the night before: 150 guests, vegetarian, ₹60,000 in total, and Dadi can't eat very spicy food. Simple, with one added sweet, fit every line. Royal didn't. I walked back in and ordered it. The owner looked disappointed. Amma was thrilled.

qa.q: How many guests were on Suraj's note?
qa.a: 150 guests.

qa.q: Why do you think Suraj stepped out to the car before deciding?
qa.a: Suraj seemed to feel pressured by the owner's tapping and the menu layout, and wanted a quiet minute to decide by the family's list instead.

qa.q: Which steps turned the decision around?
qa.a: Covering Deluxe to remove the odd option, then checking the packages against the note made with Amma: guest count, vegetarian food, the total budget and Dadi's needs.

qa.q: How might Amma feel about the way Suraj ordered?
qa.a: Amma helped make the list, so she is likely thrilled that the food fits the budget and the family's needs rather than the caterer's push. 😊

grounding: A young man removes the decoy catering package and decides by a written list of guests, budget and needs rather than the layout of the offer.

passage: I'm Zainab, Rehana's cousin, and I went with her to the wedding photographer's studio in Hyderabad last month. The man laid out a glossy brochure. Silver: ₹40,000, one photographer, soft copies. Gold: ₹75,000, two photographers, no album, no drone. Platinum: ₹78,000, two photographers, album, drone shots. 'Everyone takes Platinum, madam,' he said. I was already nodding. Rehana just folded the brochure so Gold was hidden underneath. Then she took a folded paper out of her handbag. I peeked: 'Budget 50,000. Must: good family photos, soft copies. Don't need: drone.' She read it twice, then looked only at Silver and Platinum. 'Silver, please. We'll print an album ourselves.' The man tried twice more to show Gold. Rehana didn't unfold it. Outside, she laughed and said, 'That middle one was only there for me to look at.' I still don't know how she stayed so calm.

qa.q: What did Rehana's written list say about her budget?
qa.a: Her list said 'Budget 50,000'.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling during the photographer's pitch, compared with Rehana?
qa.a: Zainab was already nodding along to Platinum, while Rehana stayed calm, which left Zainab impressed and a little puzzled.

qa.q: Which steps did Rehana take to avoid being steered, and why did they work?
qa.a: She folded the brochure to hide Gold, then compared the rest only against her written list of budget and needs, so the layout couldn't push her.

qa.q: How might the photographer have felt when Rehana wouldn't unfold the brochure?
qa.a: He was probably frustrated, since the Gold package was there to make Platinum look like the obvious choice and it didn't work on her.

grounding: A cousin watches a young woman hide the package nobody would pick and choose a photographer by her own written budget and needs.

passage:
Monday: Farhan, twenty-four and preparing for the state services exam, opened a coaching site. Recorded lectures: ₹6,000. Live classes, no mock tests: ₹11,500. Live classes with mock tests and doubt sessions: ₹12,000. 'Five hundred more for everything!' Naveen said over his shoulder. Farhan almost paid. Instead he closed the laptop.
Wednesday: at his desk he printed the page and stuck a sticky note over the middle plan. Nobody would ever pick it. Then he wrote his own list: 'Budget: 8,000. Weak area: answer writing. Need: mock tests. Don't need: live lectures, I study better alone at night.'
Saturday: he found the recorded plan could add mock tests separately for ₹1,500. Total ₹7,500. He paid it. Naveen shook his head. 'You're losing the live classes.' 'I'd have skipped them,' Farhan said, tapping his list. 'I decided with this, not with their page.'

qa.q: How much did Farhan pay in the end?
qa.a: He paid ₹7,500 for the recorded plan plus mock tests.

qa.q: Why did Farhan close the laptop on Monday instead of paying?
qa.a: He felt the pull of 'five hundred more for everything' but seemed unsure it was right for him, so he wanted time to think before deciding.

qa.q: Which steps helped Farhan decide, and why did they work?
qa.a: He covered the middle plan with a sticky note and wrote his own list of budget, weak area and needs, so he chose by his needs, not the page layout.

qa.q: How might Naveen see Farhan's final choice?
qa.a: Naveen thinks Farhan is missing out on live classes, because he is still judging by the page's offer rather than by Farhan's study habits.

grounding: Over several days a young man covers the option nobody would pick and chooses a coaching plan from a written list of his budget and needs.

passage:
You're buying your first laptop, and the shop showed you three models? Let me, your old Karthik Sir from the next desk, tell you what I learned buying my first scooter, twenty years ago.
The dealer lined up three: a basic one, a middle one that was hardly cheaper than the top, and the top one. Everyone at the shop said the top was "such value". I almost signed.
Then my father made me sit on the bench outside with a piece of paper. "Cover the middle one with your thumb," he said. "Nobody buys that. Now write what you need." I wrote: office twelve kilometres away, one passenger, my budget. The basic one fit every line.
I rode that basic scooter for nine years. So, take a pen. Write your list first. Then look at their offer.

qa.q: How far was Karthik's office when he bought the scooter?
qa.a: His office was twelve kilometres away.

qa.q: What was young Karthik feeling when he almost signed for the top scooter?
qa.a: He felt swept along and eager, persuaded by everyone calling the top one "such value".

qa.q: What was the turning point in Karthik's story?
qa.a: The turning point was sitting on the bench, covering the middle option with his thumb and writing his needs, which showed the basic scooter fit.

qa.q: How might Karthik's father have felt watching him write the list?
qa.a: His father probably felt calm and a bit proud, glad his son was learning to decide from his own needs rather than the dealer's layout.

grounding: A buyer covers the option nobody would pick, writes down his own needs and budget, and decides from the list rather than the dealer's layout.

passage:
The electronics shop was closing in ten minutes, the music was loud, and the salesman kept saying, "Last day of the offer!" Ojas and Afreen stood in front of three washing machines.
"Seven kilos, 22,000. Eight kilos, 31,000. Eight kilos with steam, 32,000," Afreen read. "The steam one, surely? Only a thousand more."
Ojas put a hand over the middle tag. "Wait. Who buys the plain eight for 31? Nobody. It's just making the steam one look cheap."
He pulled a folded paper from his pocket, the list they'd written at home: two people, small balcony, budget, no ironing fuss. "Seven kilos covers two of us. Steam is nice, but it's not on the list."
The salesman sighed. Afreen laughed. "Seven, then." They paid just as the shutters started coming down.

qa.q: What did Ojas pull from his pocket?
qa.a: He pulled a folded paper, the list they'd written at home.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he covered the middle tag?
qa.a: He felt alert and suspicious, sensing the plain eight-kilo machine was only there to make the steam one look cheap.

qa.q: Which choice worked under time pressure, and why?
qa.a: Using the list they wrote at home kept them focused on their real needs, so the closing-time rush and the decoy didn't decide for them.

qa.q: How might the salesman see Ojas and Afreen's choice?
qa.a: The salesman seems a little disappointed, since the layout usually pushes buyers to the pricier steam machine.

grounding: A buyer covers the option nobody would pick, checks the rest against a written list of needs, and decides despite a rushed, noisy shop.

passage:
The gym near Lalremsiami's office in Guwahati had a big poster at the desk: Monthly 1,500. Six months 8,500. Six months plus trainer sessions 8,900.
"Take the trainer one," said Arnab, her colleague, who had come along. "Four hundred more for a trainer!"
Lalremsiami took a photo of the poster and sat on the bench outside. She put her thumb over the middle price on the screen. Six months without a trainer at almost the same price? No one would pick that.
Then she opened her notes app and typed: I've quit gyms twice after one month. Budget: small. Need: start slowly, see if I stick.
"Monthly," she told the receptionist. "If I'm still coming in June, I'll ask about the trainer."
Arnab shrugged. "Makes sense, actually."

qa.q: How much was the six-month plan with trainer sessions?
qa.a: Six months plus trainer sessions was 8,900.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling as she sat on the bench with her notes?
qa.a: She felt calm and clear-headed, honest with herself about quitting gyms before.

qa.q: What steps helped Lalremsiami decide, and why?
qa.a: Covering the middle price and writing her own history, budget and needs let her choose from her list, not the poster.

qa.q: How might Arnab see Lalremsiami's decision?
qa.a: Arnab first pushed the trainer plan but ends up agreeing it makes sense, perhaps a bit impressed by her method.

grounding: A buyer covers the option nobody would choose, writes down her own needs and budget, and picks the monthly plan from her list.

passage:
I'm Seema, and when Joseph and I were planning our small wedding last year, the photographer sent three packages. Bronze: photos only. Silver: photos and a short video, for almost the price of Gold. Gold: photos, full video, a printed album and a drone.
Joseph said, "Gold is obviously the smart one." I felt it too. But Silver looked so pointless that I got suspicious. I printed the page and blacked Silver out with a marker. Then I wrote our list: forty guests, a church and a lunch hall, no drone needed, and the limit we had agreed on. Bronze, plus a cousin with a good phone for video, covered everything.
Joseph grumbled for a day. This year, looking at our photos, neither of us misses the drone.

qa.q: How many guests were on Seema's list?
qa.a: Forty guests.

qa.q: What did Seema feel when Silver looked so pointless?
qa.a: Seema felt suspicious, sensing the odd package was steering them towards Gold.

qa.q: What did blacking out Silver and writing a list achieve?
qa.a: It removed the decoy and let Seema and Joseph choose by their real needs and agreed limit.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel about the final choice?
qa.a: Joseph grumbled for a day, but a year later doesn't miss the drone.

grounding: A young adult recalls blacking out the package nobody would pick and deciding with a written list of needs and an agreed limit.

passage:
Purchase note, school office. Tanuja, principal.
Anirban, our new science teacher, was asked to choose a projector for Room 6 within the school budget. The vendor sent three quotes: a basic model, a mid model at nearly the top model's price with fewer features, and the top model. The mid quote was clearly there to make the top one look generous.
I watched what Anirban did. He folded the mid quote away and said, "Nobody would buy that one." Then he wrote down what Room 6 needs: bright enough for a room with big windows, a long cable, sturdy for daily use, within budget. He tested the basic one in the room at noon. It was bright enough.
He chose it and sent me the list with his reasons. I have approved it.

qa.q: Which room was the projector for?
qa.a: Room 6.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when he said "Nobody would buy that one"?
qa.a: He seemed confident and a little amused, seeing through the mid quote instead of feeling pressured by it.

qa.q: Why was testing the basic projector at noon a smart step?
qa.a: It checked the real need, brightness in a room with big windows, instead of trusting how the quotes were laid out.

qa.q: How does Tanuja see Anirban's approach?
qa.a: Tanuja approves, seeing a clear, reasoned choice based on the room's needs and the budget.

grounding: A principal's note shows a young teacher setting aside the decoy quote and choosing a projector from a written list of needs and budget.

passage:
Sunday, 9 pm

Fridge day. The showroom had three models in a row: a small single-door at 18,000, a double-door at 31,000 with no freezer drawer and a scratched door, and the big one at 32,500 with everything. Omkar was already saying, 'Only fifteen hundred more for the big one!' And I felt it too, that 'what a deal' buzz. Then I remembered Didi's trick. I took a sticky note from my bag and stuck it right over the scratched one's price card. Without it, the question was just: small or big? I typed a list on my phone: two of us, cooking every day, freezer only for peas and ice, budget 25,000. The small one ticked every line. Omkar sulked for about five minutes in the auto, then admitted the big one wouldn't fit next to the window anyway.

Preeti

passage: In the hardware shop on Nabha's grain-market road, Baljeet had three water pumps lined up on the floor. 'One horsepower, 6,500. One and a half, 11,800, no warranty. Two horsepower, 12,200, with a three-year warranty. Everyone takes the two.' Lalit felt the tug; the middle one looked silly next to the big one. He dragged an empty cement bag over the middle pump's price card. 'Now,' he said, 'just two.' Baljeet laughed. Lalit turned over an old bill and wrote: tank on the roof, one floor, Beeji's washing, the kitchen garden, what the harvest money has to cover till March. 'Will the one horsepower fill the tank in an hour?' he asked. 'Less,' Baljeet admitted. Lalit tapped the small pump. Baljeet shrugged and smiled. 'Your list, your choice.'

qa.q: What did Lalit drag over the middle pump's price card?

qa.q: What was the 'tug' Lalit felt when he heard the three prices?

passage: In a Dublin phone shop, Liam stared at the three offers on the screen. His friend Felix pointed at the most expensive. "That's the deal. Look, the middle one's nearly the same price for half the data." Liam nodded, then did something odd. He put his hand over the middle option. "Nobody would pick that one. It's just there to push us." He took out his phone notes. He had written his list the night before: calls to his mum in Poland, maps, some music, and a budget he'd set. He compared the cheap plan and the expensive one to that list, not to each other. "I don't stream on the bus. The cheap one covers it." Felix laughed. "You came prepared." "I've been caught before," Liam said.
